description: A shoulder that aches when you reach behind your back is telling you about tendon space, not damage. Take the reach test, learn how the rotator cuff tendons heal when the blade learns to move again, and get the daily plan that buys your shoulder its room back.

beats.text: ONE HAND UP, ONE HAND DOWN

scenes.narration: Stand tall. Reach one hand over your shoulder and down your back, and the other hand up from below, and try to make your fingertips meet between your shoulder blades. Do not arch your back to cheat the distance, and stop if anything pinches sharply. Now measure the gap in finger widths: how many of your own fingers fit between the two hands that cannot touch. If they overlap, your number is zero and you can stop smiling. Do both sides, because shoulders almost never match, and the bigger gap usually belongs to the shoulder that aches when you reach for a seatbelt or a back pocket. Keep your finger count. At the end, I will tell you what it means.

scenes.label: THE GAP YOUR SHOULDER CAN AFFORD
scenes.narration: Here is the line. A gap of three finger widths or less means your shoulder still owns working room: the tendons have space, the blade is helping, and the ache is a warning light, not a verdict. Beyond five fingers, the shoulder has lost its internal rotation, and every reach behind you gets paid for by tendons squeezing through a smaller doorway. Zero, fingertips touching or overlapping, is the full range the joint was built with. Most people are shocked that the two sides differ by three or four fingers. That difference is the most honest shoulder exam you will ever get for free, and it takes twenty seconds.
scenes.sub: over 5 fingers: rotation is gone - 0: fingertips meet

beats.text: A BALL ON A GOLF TEE

lines: The cuff tendons center the ball
so the big muscles can pull.
beats.title: THE CUFF

scenes.narration: Look at the design of this joint. The shoulder is a big ball balanced on a tiny socket, like a golf ball on a tee, and it only stays centered because four rotator cuff tendons hug it from every side. Those tendons run through a narrow tunnel under the bone above them. When the ball rides even slightly high or forward, the tunnel narrows, and the tendons get rubbed and squeezed with every reach. That squeeze is the ache. The tendon itself is rarely torn or broken in shoulders like yours. It is irritated tissue living in a room that got too small. Healing it does not start with resting the arm in a sling of avoidance. It starts with rebuilding the room: centering the ball, waking the cuff, and teaching the shoulder blade to move so the tunnel opens exactly when your arm needs it to.

Now the hidden half of every reach: your shoulder blade. The arm bone and the blade are partners, splitting every big arm movement between them in a rhythm. When you reach behind your back, the blade is supposed to tilt and glide to open space for the tendons. But desk life glues blades down. Hours of sitting round the shoulders forward, the blade tips the wrong way, and it stops showing up for its half of the movement. The arm then has to steal the missing motion from the joint itself, and the tendons pay the difference in the tunnel. This is why stretching the arm alone so rarely fixes the ache. The arm was never the whole machine. Wake the blade up with wall slides and rows, and the doorway the tendons live in gets bigger on every reach, without anyone ever touching the tendon. You can prove this in ten seconds. Reach behind your back right now and note the gap. Then shrug the shoulder blade up and back, set it, and reach again. The gap shrinks, not because your arm changed in ten seconds, but because the foundation moved. That tiny experiment is this entire episode in miniature.

So how does an irritated cuff tendon actually get loaded without getting rubbed? Isometrics again, the quiet load. Press your fist into a wall with the arm in a comfortable position and hold: the cuff tendons pull hard, the joint does not move, and nothing grinds through the tunnel. Sustained holds like this are the standard first chapter of tendon rehab because they feed the tissue its rebuilding signal at zero friction cost. Once holds are calm, slow movement through the pain-free arc teaches the new collagen to work in real positions. The painful arc itself, that pinch at the top of a reach, gets trained last and gently, as the room grows. Order matters more than intensity. A healing tendon is not impressed by your toughness. It is convinced by your sequencing.

beats.text: YOUR ARM IS A LIGHT LEVER

scenes.narration: Here is the skinny advantage at the shoulder. Your arm is a light lever. Every wall slide, every slow reach, every press into the doorframe loads your cuff with a fraction of what a heavily muscled arm drags through that tunnel. That means you can practice the blade rhythm and the cuff holds every single day, in small doses, without the practice itself becoming an irritation. Shoulder tendons heal on frequency, not heroics, and your build is a frequency machine. The big guy has to plan his shoulder rehab like a workout. You can scatter yours through the day like a habit, three calm minutes at a time, and let the tunnel remodel while he is still warming up.

Train with me. Back against the wall, arms in a goalpost, slide up slowly keeping wrists and elbows touching, only as high as nothing pinches. Forty seconds of gliding, twenty of rest, three rounds. The blade does the work.

Here is your week. Wall slides every day, two or three easy sets, always stopping below the pinch. Cuff press holds three days a week: fist into the wall, arm low and comfortable, thirty second holds in a few directions. Reach practice in the shower's warm water, where everything is calm, letting the gap close on its own schedule. Sleep off the sore side for now; a tendon being squeezed all night starts every day in debt. The mistakes to retire: stretching by forcing the arm up the back toward the pinch, retired. Overhead pressing through the ache to prove a point, retired. Ignoring the blade because it has no mirror appeal, retired. And the rule: if the shoulder is weak, if you cannot lift the arm, if pain wakes you nightly or follows a fall or injury, see a professional if it persists. Weakness plus pain is a different story than ache alone, and it deserves imaging, not patience.

So, your gap. Over five fingers: the blade is stuck and the tunnel is small, and the daily slides plus holds are not optional extras, they are the whole treatment. Three to five: the room is growing back, keep the frequency and stop testing the pinch every hour. Under three, or zero: your shoulder owns its room again, and maintenance is a minute of slides a day. Comment your gap for both sides, just the numbers. In thirty days we reach again and measure the new doorway. Shoulders do not heal by being left alone in a smaller room. They heal when the room gets rebuilt around them.

Your shoulder is not worn out. Its room just got small, and rooms can be rebuilt. Glide the blade a little every day, and in thirty days we measure again together. Subscribe so the retest finds you. This is {channel}. Train the cable.

title: Stop Doing shoulder ache Wrong: Train Your shoulder tendon healing Instead
